segments: 414 Chronography of Bar Hebraeus {Bar 'Ebraya}.
and they asked them their prices.
Now one of those merchants, whose name was Ahmad,
demanded for something he had bought for ten dinars
three balishes {bīsadhyē} of silver,
each balish being seven hundred zuzē.
When Genghis Khan heard this, he was angry and said:
"Does this man perhaps think that we have never seen a garment at all?" And he signaled to the treasurers,
and they brought out many gold-embroidered garments and showed them to those merchants.
And the king ordered that that merchant be imprisoned,
and that everything he had with him be written down.
And they brought his two other companions,
and inspected their wares,
and asked their prices.
They, however, did not show any prices at all,
but said:
"We have brought these wares
in the name of the Khan;
if he is gracious and gives us something, he knows best."
And their word pleased the Khan,
and he commanded that they be given
for each gold-embroidered garment {maddah OCR? for mdahbā} one balish of gold,
that is, seven hundred mithqals,
and for every two pieces of cotton cloth {‘amarkūbā} one balish of silver.
And he also showed mercy to that other companion of theirs,
and gave to him as well, like them.
And the Khan commanded the queens and his sons and daughters
to give gold to their servants and send them with these three merchants,
to bring them wares.
And they did so.
And about four hundred merchant men assembled,
and an envoy was sent with them to Sultan Muhammad of Persia, saying to him:
"Henceforth, it has pleased us that there be peace between the kingdoms in all the earth,
and that merchants may go and come without fear,
and the rich and the poor may live in peace and give thanks to God."
And when the envoy set out with the merchants and they reached Otrar, a city of the Persians,
the governor of that city sent and informed the Sultan of the matter.
And that Sultan, having become covetous of what they had with them,
commanded that governor whose name was Inalchuq {Inashluq} to put them all to death secretly.
And when he had done so,
one of them, by divine providence, escaped,
and went and informed Genghis Khan.
And when he heard this report,
he was inflamed with wrath.
And alone he went up onto the top of a certain mountain,
and uncovered his head,
and put his face to the dust of the ground {ar'a OCR?}.
And he remained there for three days,
neither eating nor drinking.
